E is the strongest. It has the most restraint: the blow is given in two sentences, and the "I will not describe the rest" instinct is honoured throughout. The voice is the most believable, carried by small, physical details: the watch he has never corrected "from vanity," the waistcoat where the proof sits, Odile who "in thirty years has never once asked me where I have been." The clockwork is explained in the course of the confession rather than announced, and the ending lands on Félix and "it was not Félix's fault that he did not," followed by the flat "I have no more to add."

B is close behind. Its ending, "Each year at dinner he told me my watch ran fast. It did.", is the best closing line in the set, and "A house of this kind keeps its own time" makes the lesson of the witnesses land without a speech. The Sunday detail even checks out against the calendar.

C has a warm, believable voice and a strong beat in "She was only listening for me." Its weaknesses are the exoneration paragraph, which tidies up the other suspects a little too neatly, and a Latin tag that slightly undercuts the ending.

D is precise and credible for a physician, but the timestamp ledger reads more like an exhibit than a confession. It is clear without lecturing, but it has less feeling and its ending is merely adequate.

F has the best single observation, that a repeater cannot be made to unsay what it has said. But it lectures on Temple time, stacks aphorisms, and ends on a grammar joke that is too clever for a man in this situation.

A is weakest. It has a good ending line, but the paragraph of red herrings (Girard, Félix's brandy, Lina, Rosa) makes the clockwork muddy and turns the letter into an accounting. "Tempora mutantur" and the "old rules" line moralise where restraint was needed.
